Every one of them optimized a **model**: a transition function, a reward, a start distribution. Before a policy flies an aircraft or trades money, we need evidence that it does what we want in the world, not just in the model. **Policy validation** asks how well a policy performs on the metrics we care about, how sure we are of that answer, and how the answer changes when the model is wrong. This chapter closes Part II. Part III ([Chapter 15](../part3/ch15-exploration-and-exploitation.qmd) on) drops the assumption that the model is known at all. **The question:** how do we measure a policy's safety and performance, especially for rare failures, and how do we find the situations in which it breaks? The short answer: **evaluate the metrics exactly when the problem is small, and by simulation when it isn't, always with error bars.** Rare failures need **importance sampling**, which simulates dangerous situations more often and then corrects for it. **Robustness analysis** re-evaluates the policy on models that differ from the one it was optimized for. **Trade analysis** maps the compromises between metrics, such as safety and nuisance alerts. **Adversarial analysis** searches for the most likely way the policy fails. ```{dot} //| label: fig-ch14-map //| fig-width: 7 //| fig-height: 4.6 //| fig-cap: "Map of this chapter. If the score adds up step by step, **policy evaluation** (Chapter 7) computes it exactly. Otherwise, or when the state space is too large, we **simulate** and average. 2. **Every estimate needs an error bar.** The **standard error** $\hat\sigma / \sqrt{n}$ says how far the average of $n$ simulations typically is from the truth. For a rare event, the **relative** standard error matters: an estimate of $10^{-4}$ that is off by $10^{-4}$ is useless, however small that error looks. 3. **Importance sampling for rare events.** Draw trajectories from a **proposal** that makes failures common, and weight each by how much more likely it was under the proposal than under the real model. The weighted average is still unbiased. The ideal proposal samples trajectories in proportion to how much they contribute. A proposal that pushes too hard produces a few enormous weights and can be worse than no proposal at all. 4. **Robustness.** A policy is only as good as its model. Re-evaluate it on plausible variations: noisier dynamics, a pilot who doesn't always comply. **Robust dynamic programming** optimizes against the worst model in a set. 5. **Trade analysis.** Safety and efficiency compete. Varying a policy's design parameters traces out the achievable pairs of metrics. Policies that are beaten on every metric by another policy are **dominated**; the rest form the **Pareto front**. 6. **Adversarial analysis.** Let an adversary choose the random outcomes, balancing "cause a failure" against "stay plausible". The result is the **most likely failure**: a concrete story that engineers can inspect and judge. ### Vocabulary | Term | Plain meaning | |:---|:---| | Trajectory metric $f_{\text{traj}}(\tau)$ | A score for one simulated trajectory, such as 1 if it ends in a collision | | Performance metric $f(\pi)$ | The expected trajectory metric under policy $\pi$ | | Standard error (SE) | Typical distance between a sample average and the true mean | | Relative standard error | Standard error divided by the estimate; what matters for rare events | | Proposal distribution $P'(\tau)$ | The distribution we actually sample from in importance sampling | | Importance weight $w$ | $P(\tau)/P'(\tau)$: corrects for sampling from the proposal | | Effective sample size | How many unweighted samples the weighted ones are worth | | Robust dynamic programming | Choose actions against the worst model in a set | | Pareto front | The policies that no other policy beats on every metric | | Most likely failure | The highest-probability trajectory that ends in failure | : Terms used on this page. {#tbl-vocab} ### After this chapter you can - Evaluate a policy's metrics exactly by policy evaluation, or by simulation with standard errors and confidence intervals. - Estimate a rare-event probability with importance sampling, and recognize a proposal that makes things worse. - Stress-test a policy on models it wasn't designed for, and use robust dynamic programming. - Build a trade-off curve and identify the Pareto front. - Turn a policy into an adversarial search problem and find its most likely failure. ## Intuition ::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"} A bridge has been designed on a computer. Before opening it, engineers: - **Measure its performance** under typical traffic, and report the figure with a margin of error. - **Look for rare failures** by loading the model with heavy trucks far more often than real traffic would, then scaling the results back down. - **Check robustness:** what if the steel is 10% weaker than specified? - **Weigh trade-offs:** a stiffer bridge is safer but costs more; which designs are not beaten on both counts? - **Play the adversary:** what is the most plausible combination of wind, load and fatigue that brings it down? Each check can send the design back to the drawing board. ::: Our running example is **aircraft collision avoidance** (ADM Appendix F.6, in the [problem gallery](../appendices/f-problems.qmd#collision-avoidance)). Our aircraft flies head on toward an intruder, which it would meet in 40 seconds. The state is our altitude $h$ relative to the intruder, our vertical rate $\dot h$, the previous advisory, and the time left $t_{\text{col}}$. Every second the policy issues an advisory: none, descend at 5 m/s, or climb at 5 m/s. The pilot changes the vertical rate by at most 1 m/s per second, and random gusts add $\pm 2$ m/s with probability ¼ each. A **collision** means passing within 50 m vertically. Each change of advisory costs 0.01, a collision costs 1. We compare two policies: - the **optimal** policy for those costs, found by backward induction (Chapter 7); - a **simple** policy: when the intruder is within 50 m vertically and less than 30 s away, climb if we are above it and descend if below. Because the starting $h$ and $\dot h$ are whole numbers here, and every change is a whole number, the state stays on an integer grid. That makes exact evaluation possible, so every estimate on this page can be checked against the true answer. ### Scoring a policy From starts spread uniformly over $\pm 200$ m and $\pm 10$ m/s, the optimal policy collides with probability 6\.42e\-04 and changes its advisory 0\.34 times per encounter on average. The simple policy collides with probability 0\.072 and changes advisories 0\.98 times. Both numbers are exact: they come from policy evaluation, the same backward sweep that computes a value function, but scoring collisions and changes instead of rewards. See @eq-metric and @eq-additive. ### How sure are we? Simulating 10,000 encounters of the optimal policy gave 5 collisions: an estimate of 5\.0e\-04 with standard error 2\.2e\-04. That's a **relative** error of 45%. To bring it down to 10%, direct simulation needs about 155\,759 encounters. Meanwhile the average number of advisory changes, a common event, is already pinned down to 1\.4% after 10,000. See @eq-standard-error. ### Make failures common, then correct Instead of waiting for gusts to cause a collision, sample gusts that are more likely to cause one, and weight each simulated encounter by how much less likely it was in reality. A crude version, "push toward the intruder a bit more often", cuts the error only a little: its relative error is 27% against 36% for direct sampling. Pushing much harder makes it worse (92%). A proposal guided by an estimate of the risk from each state does far better: 4\.5% with the risk computed from a deliberately wrong model (@fig-importance). See @eq-importance and @eq-optimal-proposal. ### What if the model is wrong? The optimal policy assumed the pilot always follows the advisory. If the pilot complies only 80% of the time, its collision probability rises to 3\.8e\-03, about 6 times higher. A policy optimized against the worse of the two models (always complies, or complies 80% of the time) keeps it at 1\.4e\-03, at the price of more advisory changes (@fig-robustness). See @eq-robust. ### Safety costs alerts Lowering the cost of an advisory change makes the optimal policy more cautious: safer, but more disruptive. Plotting collision probability against advisory changes for many policies shows the achievable compromises. Of the 96 simple threshold policies we tried, 100% are beaten by some optimal policy on both metrics at once (@fig-trade). See @eq-pareto. ### How does it fail? An adversary that controls the gusts can always cause a collision. The question is how *unlikely* its gusts must be. For the optimal policy, every start needs at least 3 gusts, each half as likely as calm air. For the simple policy, 2\.0% of starts end in a collision with no gust at all (@fig-adversary). See @eq-adversarial. ## Formalism ### Performance metrics A trajectory $\tau = (s_1, a_1, s_2, \ldots)$ produced by policy $\pi$ from a start distribution $b$ gets a score $f_{\text{traj}}(\tau)$. The policy's **performance metric** is its expectation (ADM §14.1): ::: {.key-equation data-name="Performance metric"} $$ f(\pi) = \mathbb{E}_\tau\big[f_{\text{traj}}(\tau)\big], \qquad P(\tau) = b(s_1) \prod_t T\big(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, \pi(s_t)\big) $$ {#eq-metric} ::: **In words.** Average the score over all the trajectories the policy can produce, each weighted by its probability. **Term by term.** - $b(s_1)$ is the probability of the start state. - Each factor $T(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, \pi(s_t))$ is the probability of one transition when following the policy. - With $f_{\text{traj}} = 1$ for a collision and 0 otherwise, $f(\pi)$ is the collision probability. The expectation is only one summary. Tail measures, such as the 5th percentile of the return or the mean of the worst 5%, can matter more for safety. When the score adds up over steps, the expectation is a value function: ::: {.key-equation data-name="Additive metrics by policy evaluation"} $$ f_{\text{traj}}(\tau) = \sum_t f_{\text{step}}(s_t, a_t), \qquad f(\pi) = \sum_s f_{\text{state}}(s)\, b(s) $$ {#eq-additive} ::: **In words.** If the score is a sum of per-step scores, treat the per-step score as a reward. Policy evaluation then gives its expected total from every state, $f_{\text{state}}$. Average that over the start distribution. **Term by term.** Advisory changes are additive: $f_{\text{step}} = 1$ when $a_t \ne a_{t-1}$. Collision is additive too, with a single nonzero term at $t_{\text{col}} = 0$. In the code, `evaluate` runs this backward sweep for any per-step and final score. **Why it holds.** Linearity of expectation: the expected sum is the sum of expected per-step scores. That is exactly the quantity a value function computes when the reward is $f_{\text{step}}$ (Chapter 7, with $\gamma = 1$ over a finite horizon). ### Error bars for simulation With $n$ simulated trajectory scores $x_1, \ldots, x_n$, sample mean $\hat\mu$ and sample standard deviation $\hat\sigma$: ::: {.key-equation .famous data-name="Standard error and relative standard error"} $$ \text{SE} = \frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt n}, \qquad \text{relative SE} = \frac{\hat\sigma}{\hat\mu\sqrt n}, \qquad \text{95\% interval: } \hat\mu \pm 1.96\,\text{SE} $$ {#eq-standard-error} ::: **In words.** The average of $n$ samples wanders around the true mean by about $\hat\sigma/\sqrt n$. Quadrupling the sample size halves the error. **Term by term.** - $\hat\sigma$ is the spread of individual trajectory scores. For a 0/1 event with probability $p$, it is $\sqrt{p(1-p)}$. - For that event, the relative SE is $\sqrt{(1-p)/(np)} \approx 1/\sqrt{np}$: one over the square root of the *number of failures observed*. Ten failures give about 32% relative error, a hundred about 10%. - The normal interval can extend below 0 for a rare event. The Bayesian alternative from Chapter 4, a $\text{Beta}(1 + k, 1 + n - k)$ posterior after $k$ failures in $n$ trials, never does. **Why it holds.** The variance of a sum of $n$ independent samples is $n\sigma^2$, so the variance of their average is $\sigma^2/n$. The central limit theorem makes the average approximately normal, which gives the 1.96. ### Importance sampling To estimate $f(\pi)$ from trajectories drawn from a **proposal** $P'$ instead of $P$ (ADM §14.2): ::: {.key-equation .famous data-name="Importance sampling"} $$ f(\pi) = \sum_\tau f_{\text{traj}}(\tau)\, P(\tau) = \sum_\tau f_{\text{traj}}(\tau)\, \frac{P(\tau)}{P'(\tau)}\, P'(\tau) \approx \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n f_{\text{traj}}(\tau^{(i)})\, \frac{P(\tau^{(i)})}{P'(\tau^{(i)})}, \quad \tau^{(i)} \sim P' $$ {#eq-importance} ::: **In words.** Sample from a distribution that produces the interesting trajectories more often, and down-weight each one by how much more often it was produced than it should have been. **Term by term.** - $w^{(i)} = P(\tau^{(i)})/P'(\tau^{(i)})$ is the **importance weight**. A failure that the proposal makes 100 times more likely counts $1/100$. - $P'$ must give positive probability to every trajectory that $P$ does and that has $f_{\text{traj}} \neq 0$. Otherwise those trajectories are never seen, and the estimate is biased. - With $P(\tau)$ from @eq-metric, the start and policy terms cancel if the proposal only changes the noise. The weight is then a product of per-step ratios $P(\nu_t)/P'(\nu_t)$. That's what `simulate` accumulates, in logs. **Why it holds.** Multiplying and dividing by $P'(\tau)$ changes nothing. The second sum is an expectation under $P'$, and a sample average estimates it without bias. This is the same idea as likelihood weighting in Bayesian networks (Chapter 3). Which proposal is best? ::: {.key-equation data-name="Optimal proposal"} $$ P^*(\tau) = \frac{|f_{\text{traj}}(\tau)|\, P(\tau)}{\sum_{\tau'} |f_{\text{traj}}(\tau')|\, P(\tau')}, \qquad P'(\nu \mid s) \propto P(\nu)\, \hat U\big(s'(s, \nu)\big) $$ {#eq-optimal-proposal} ::: **In words.** The ideal proposal samples each trajectory in proportion to its contribution to the answer. For a sequential problem, that can be done one step at a time: choose each random outcome in proportion to its probability times the risk that remains afterward. **Term by term.** - For a nonnegative $f_{\text{traj}}$ the denominator of $P^*$ is $f(\pi)$ itself, the unknown. So $P^*$ is a target to approximate, not something we can use directly. - On the right, $\hat U(s')$ is an estimate of the risk-to-go: the probability of a failure from the next state $s'$ onward. With the exact risk-to-go this reproduces $P^*$ and every weighted sample equals the start state's risk, so the estimate's only noise is from the start states. With an approximate $\hat U$ (here, computed from a model with larger gusts), it is still very good. - We add a small constant to $\hat U$ so that no outcome gets probability 0 (the support condition above). **Why it holds.** Under $P^*$ with $f_{\text{traj}} \ge 0$, every sample's weighted value is $f_{\text{traj}}(\tau)P(\tau)/P^*(\tau) = f(\pi)$: zero variance. For the step-by-step form, write the risk-to-go as $U(s) = \sum_\nu P(\nu)\, U(s'(s, \nu))$. Choosing $\nu$ with probability $P(\nu)U(s')/U(s)$ gives a step weight of $U(s)/U(s')$. Along a failing trajectory these ratios telescope to $U(s_1)/U(s_{\text{end}}) = U(s_1)$, because the final risk of a failure is 1. ### Robustness and robust dynamic programming Evaluate the policy on models other than the one it was optimized for: stress testing (ADM §14.3). If it is too sensitive, optimize against a set of models $(T_1, R_1), \ldots, (T_n, R_n)$ at once (G. N. Iyengar, *Mathematics of Operations Research*, 2005): ::: {.key-equation data-name="Robust Bellman update"} $$ U_{k+1}(s) = \max_a\ \min_i\ \Big(R_i(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T_i(s' \mid s, a)\, U_k(s')\Big) $$ {#eq-robust} ::: **In words.** Score each action by the model that is worst for it, then pick the action with the best worst case. **Term by term.** - The $\min_i$ is taken separately for each state and action: the "worst model" can differ from place to place. - With a single model, this is the ordinary Bellman update (Chapter 7). - In the code we minimize cost rather than maximize reward, so the update reads $\min_a \max_i$. **Why it holds.** It is the Bellman update of a game in which nature picks the model after seeing our action. The result guarantees at least $U(s)$ against any sequence of models chosen from the set. ### Trade analysis For several metrics $f_1, \ldots, f_k$, all to be minimized (ADM §14.4): ::: {.key-equation data-name="Pareto dominance"} $$ \pi' \text{ dominates } \pi \iff f_j(\pi') \le f_j(\pi) \text{ for all } j \text{ and } f_j(\pi') < f_j(\pi) \text{ for some } j $$ {#eq-pareto} ::: **In words.** One policy dominates another if it is at least as good on every metric and strictly better on one. The **Pareto front** is the set of policies nothing dominates. **Term by term.** Metrics to be maximized are negated first. Dominated policies can be discarded whatever the relative importance of the metrics. Choosing among the policies on the front is a value judgment, such as how many nuisance alerts one avoided collision is worth. A single weighted objective $\theta f_1 + (1 - \theta) f_2$, optimized for each $\theta$, traces part of the front. That is what varying the cost of an advisory change does in @fig-trade. ### Adversarial analysis Turn validation into search (ADM §14.5). An adversary picks the next state as its action, among those our policy can lead to. Its reward is ::: {.key-equation data-name="Adversarial reward"} $$ R'(s, s') = -R\big(s, \pi(s)\big) + \lambda \log T\big(s' \mid s, \pi(s)\big) $$ {#eq-adversarial} ::: **In words.** The adversary wants us to do badly, but pays for every unlikely outcome it chooses. $\lambda$ sets the exchange rate between our loss and plausibility. **Term by term.** - $-R$ is our cost, so the adversary gains when we lose. - $\log T$ is the log-probability of the outcome it chose. Summed over the trajectory, it is the trajectory's log-likelihood. - Small $\lambda$: the adversary causes a failure whatever it takes. Large $\lambda$: it follows the most likely trajectory, failure or not. - The adversarial transitions are deterministic (the next state is the adversary's action), so this is a search problem that dynamic programming solves exactly on our lattice. - This $\lambda$ is unrelated to GAE's $\lambda$ in Chapter 13. To find the **most likely failure**, keep only the log-probabilities as rewards and require the trajectory to end in a failure: a terminal reward of 0 for a failure and $-\infty$ otherwise (eq. 14.16 in the book). The answer is the highest-probability trajectory among those that fail. ## Worked example ### Error bars by hand The first 10,000 simulated encounters of the optimal policy contained $k =$ 5 collisions. - **Estimate:** $\hat\mu = k/n =$ 5\.0e\-04. - **Spread:** $\hat\sigma \approx \sqrt{\hat\mu(1 - \hat\mu)} =$ 0\.0224. - **Standard error:** $\hat\sigma/\sqrt{10{,}000} =$ 2\.2e\-04, a relative error of 45%. - **95% normal interval:** (6\.2e\-05, 9\.4e\-04). The Beta posterior's 95% interval is (2\.2e\-04, 1\.2e\-03). The true value, from exact evaluation, is 6\.42e\-04. Both intervals contain it, but both are wide: the upper end is 15 times the lower end for the normal interval and 5\.3 times for the Beta interval. ### One importance weight Take a state below the intruder ($h < 0$), where an upward push of +2 m/s is "toward" it. The tilt proposal with strength 1 multiplies each outcome's probability by $e^{+1}$ (toward), $e^0$ (calm) or $e^{-1}$ (away), then renormalizes: | Outcome | $P(\nu)$ | $P'(\nu)$ | Ratio $P/P'$ | |---|---|---|---| | away, −2 | 0.25 | 0\.072 | 3\.46 | | calm, 0 | 0.50 | 0\.393 | 1\.27 | | toward, +2 | 0.25 | 0\.534 | 0\.47 | : Tilted noise below the intruder. {#tbl-tilt} Three steps with outcomes toward, calm, toward get weight 0\.47 × 1\.27 × 0\.47 = 0\.278. Over 40 steps these factors multiply. A trajectory with many "away" steps gets a weight of 3\.5 per step, so a handful of such trajectories can carry enormous weight. That is why a strong tilt made the estimate *worse*. ### Who dominates whom? Four policies, scored exactly (collision probability, advisory changes): ::: {#0a8f2b1b .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=3} | Policy | Collision probability | Advisory changes | On the front? | |---|---|---|---| | simple, 50 m / 30 s | 7.25e-02 | 0.98 | no | | simple, 150 m / 30 s | 2.43e-03 | 1.38 | no | | simple, 200 m / 40 s | 2.08e-04 | 1.89 | yes | | optimal, change cost 0.01 | 6.42e-04 | 0.34 | yes | ::: ::: The optimal policy has both fewer collisions and fewer changes than the first two simple policies, so it dominates them. The 200 m / 40 s simple policy has fewer collisions than the optimal one, but it changes advisories much more often, so neither dominates the other. Among these four, the front is the optimal policy and that one simple policy. ## Interactive ### Explore the trade-off Move the simple policy's thresholds and see where it lands among all the policies of @fig-trade. Returns (mean, se, relative_se, (low, high)).""" x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float) mean = x.mean() se = x.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(x)) # sample sd / sqrt(n) z = stats.norm.ppf(0.5 + level / 2) # 1.96 for 95% rel = se / mean if mean != 0 else np.inf return mean, se, rel, (mean - z * se, mean + z * se) def beta_interval(k: int, n: int, level: float = 0.95): """Bayesian interval for a probability after k successes in n trials, from the Beta(1 + k, 1 + n - k) posterior of a uniform prior (Ch 4). Unlike the normal interval, it never goes below 0.""" post = stats.beta(1 + k, 1 + n - k) return post.ppf(0.5 - level / 2), post.ppf(0.5 + level / 2) def evaluate(model, policy, step_metric=None, final_metric=None, history=False): """Exact policy evaluation of an additive metric (eq. 14.3) by backward induction. step_metric(a_prev, a) scores each step (default: 0) and final_metric is a (n_h, n_hdot) array scored at t_col = 0 (default: the collision indicator). Returns V[a_prev, i_h, i_hdot] at t_col = T_START: the expected total from each start state. With history=True, returns the list of V at t_col = 0, 1, ..., T_START. """ final = collided(model) if final_metric is None else final_metric V = np.repeat(final[None], 3, axis=0) Vs = [V] a_prev = np.arange(3)[:, None, None] i = np.arange(V.shape[1])[:, None] # row index, broadcasts j = np.arange(V.shape[2])[None, :] # column index for t in range(1, T_START + 1): EV = expect(model, V) # (a, n_h, n_hdot) a = policy[t] # (a_prev, n_h, n_hdot) V = EV[a, i, j] # V[p, i, j] = EV[a[p, i, j], i, j] if step_metric is not None: V = V + step_metric(a_prev, a) Vs.append(V) return Vs if history else V ``` ## Julia ```{.julia .snippet} using ADM, Random, Statistics import Distributions # Mean, standard error (eq. 14.5), relative standard error (eq. 14.6), 95% interval. function mc_estimate(x) μ, se = mean(x), std(x) / sqrt(length(x)) # std uses n - 1, like ddof=1 return μ, se, se / μ, (μ - 1.96se, μ + 1.96se) end # Bayesian interval after k successes in n trials: Beta(1 + k, 1 + n - k) posterior. beta_interval(k, n) = Distributions.quantile.(Distributions.Beta(1 + k, 1 + n - k), (0.025, 0.975)) m = CAModel() policy, _ = ca_optimal_policy(m) exact = ca_start_average(m, ca_evaluate(m, policy)) # exact, by policy evaluation # Direct simulation from uniform integer starts. rng = MersenneTwister(0) # Float64 turns each true/false into 1.0/0.0 so mean and std are ordinary numbers. hits = [Float64(abs(ca_simulate(m, policy, rand(rng, -CA_H_START:CA_H_START), rand(rng, -CA_HDOT_START:CA_HDOT_START), rng)[1]) < CA_COLLISION_H) for _ in 1:100_000] μ, se, rel, ci = mc_estimate(hits) println("exact $(round(exact; sigdigits = 3)), estimate $(round(μ; sigdigits = 3)) ± $(round(se; sigdigits = 2))") @assert abs(μ - exact) < 4se @assert beta_interval(sum(hits), length(hits))[1] > 0 ``` ::: ### Importance sampling ::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"} ## Python ```python def importance_estimate(f: Array, log_w: Array): """Importance sampling estimate of E_P[f] from samples drawn from a proposal P', with log_w = log P(tau) - log P'(tau) (eq. 14.12). Returns (mean, se, ess). The effective sample size ess = (sum w)^2 / sum w^2 says how many direct samples the weighted ones are worth for estimating the weights' spread; it collapses when a few huge weights dominate. """ w = np.exp(np.asarray(log_w, dtype=float)) fw = np.asarray(f, dtype=float) * w # each sample's contribution n = len(fw) return fw.mean(), fw.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n), w.sum()**2 / (w**2).sum() def simulate(model, policy, h, hdot, rng, tilt=0.0, guide=None, eps=1e-6, record=False): """Roll out len(h) episodes side by side from integer starts h, hdot. By default the noise is drawn from the model. Two proposals bias it toward collisions, for importance sampling: tilt > 0: P'(nu) is proportional to P(nu) exp(tilt * s), where s = +1 for a push toward the intruder (it reduces |h|), -1 for a push away and 0 for nu = 0; guide: risk-to-go tables from evaluate(..., history=True). P'(nu) is proportional to P(nu) (guide[t-1](next state) + eps): eq. 14.13 applied one step at a time. eps keeps every branch possible. The returned log weights, sum log P(nu) / P'(nu), undo the bias (eq. 14.12); without a proposal they are all 0. Returns (h_final, changes, log_w), plus the (n, T_START + 1) altitude paths when record is True. The dynamics are exact (no clamping); only the policy lookup clamps to the lattice. """ h, hdot = np.array(h), np.array(hdot) n = len(h) a_prev = np.zeros(n, dtype=int) changes, log_w = np.zeros(n), np.zeros(n) path = [h.copy()] nus, p_nu = zip(*model.noise_outcomes()) for t in range(T_START, 0, -1): a = policy[t][(a_prev,) + _index(model, h, hdot)] changes += a != a_prev comply = rng.random(n) < model.compliance acc = np.zeros(n, dtype=int) for k in (1, 2): # advised rates; "none" keeps 0 m = comply & (a == k) acc[m] = accel(model, hdot[m], k) h2 = h + hdot # the next altitude uses the old rate # Proposal weight of each noise value, shape (3, n), unnormalized. w = np.array([np.full(n, p) for p in p_nu]) if tilt: toward = -np.sign(h) # +1 below the intruder, -1 above w *= np.exp(tilt * np.sign(nus)[:, None] * toward) if guide is not None: for k, nu in enumerate(nus): # guide[t - 1][a_prev', i_h', i_hdot'] with a_prev' = a. w[k] *= guide[t - 1][(a,) + _index(model, h2, hdot + acc + nu)] + eps q = w / w.sum(axis=0) # proposal probabilities P'(nu) # Inverse-CDF draw of the branch: count the cumulative # probabilities below u (the min guards against rounding). k = np.minimum((rng.random(n) > np.cumsum(q, axis=0)).sum(axis=0), 2) log_w += np.log(np.take(p_nu, k)) - np.log(q[k, np.arange(n)]) h, hdot, a_prev = h2, hdot + acc + np.take(nus, k), a path.append(h.copy()) out = (h, changes, log_w) return out + (np.array(path).T,) if record else out ``` ## Julia ```{.julia .snippet} using ADM, Random, Statistics m = CAModel() policy, _ = ca_optimal_policy(m) risk = ca_evaluate(m, policy; history = true) # risk[t + 1]: risk-to-go at t_col = t exact = ca_start_average(m, risk[end]) # One guided encounter: choose each gust with probability ∝ P(ν) (risk after it + ε) # (eq. 14.13 one step at a time) and return (collided?, log weight). function guided_rollout(h, ḣ, rng; ε = 1e-6) a_prev, logw = 1, 0.0 noise = ADM.ca_noise(m) # ((ν, P(ν)) for ν = -2, 0, 2) for t in CA_T_START:-1:1 a = policy[t][a_prev, ca_index(m, h, ḣ)...] acc = ADM.ca_accel(m, ḣ, a) # Proposal weights: P(ν) times the risk-to-go of the state after ν. w = [p * (risk[t][a, ca_index(m, h + ḣ, ḣ + acc + ν)...] + ε) for (ν, p) in noise] q = w ./ sum(w) k = min(searchsortedfirst(cumsum(q), rand(rng)), 3) # inverse-CDF draw logw += log(noise[k][2]) - log(q[k]) # log P(ν) - log P'(ν) h, ḣ, a_prev = h + ḣ, ḣ + acc + noise[k][1], a end return abs(h) < CA_COLLISION_H, logw end # Importance sampling estimate (eq. 14.12): mean of f × w, with its standard error. function importance_estimate(f, logw) fw = f .* exp.(logw) return mean(fw), std(fw) / sqrt(length(fw)) end rng = MersenneTwister(1) runs = [guided_rollout(rand(rng, -200:200), rand(rng, -10:10), rng) for _ in 1:2_000] μ, se = importance_estimate(first.(runs), last.(runs)) println("exact $(round(exact; sigdigits = 4)), guided estimate $(round(μ; sigdigits = 4)) ± $(round(se; sigdigits = 2))") @assert abs(μ - exact) < 4se && se < 0.05exact ``` ::: ### Robustness and trade-offs ::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"} ## Python ```python def optimal_policy(model=Model(), models=None): """Backward induction for the minimum expected cost. Returns (policy, cost): policy[t, a_prev, i_h, i_hdot] is the advisory at t_col = t (row 0 is unused) and cost[a_prev, i_h, i_hdot] is the optimal expected cost at t_col = T_START. With `models`, a list of Models, it is robust dynamic programming: each advisory is scored by its worst model, then the best advisory is chosen. """ models = models or [model] change = model.change_cost * (1 - np.eye(3)) # change[a_prev, a] U = np.repeat(model.collision_cost * collided(model)[None], 3, axis=0) policy = np.zeros((T_START + 1,) + U.shape, dtype=np.int8) for t in range(1, T_START + 1): EU = np.max([expect(m, U) for m in models], axis=0) # worst model # Q[a_prev, a, ...]: cost of switching to a, then continuing. Q = change[:, :, None, None] + EU[None] policy[t] = Q.argmin(axis=1) U = Q.min(axis=1) return policy, U def pareto_front(points: Array) -> Array: """Boolean mask of the rows of points (n, k) that no other row dominates, where every metric is to be minimized. Row j dominates row i if it is no worse on every metric and better on at least one.""" P = np.asarray(points, dtype=float) # no_worse[i, j]: row j is <= row i everywhere; better: < somewhere. no_worse = (P[None, :, :] <= P[:, None, :]).all(axis=2) better = (P[None, :, :] < P[:, None, :]).any(axis=2) return ~(no_worse & better).any(axis=1) ``` ## Julia ```{.julia .snippet} using ADM # Rows of `points` that no other row dominates (all metrics minimized, eq. on Pareto dominance). function pareto_front(points) n = size(points, 1) dominates(j, i) = all(points[j, :] .<= points[i, :]) && any(points[j, :] .< points[i, :]) return [!any(dominates(j, i) for j in 1:n if j != i) for i in 1:n] end m, worse = CAModel(), CAModel(compliance = 0.8) nominal, _ = ca_optimal_policy(m) robust, _ = ca_optimal_policy(m; models = [m, worse]) # robust dynamic programming (eq. 14.14) collision(policy, model) = ca_start_average(model, ca_evaluate(model, policy)) advisory_changes(policy) = ca_start_average(m, ca_evaluate(m, policy; step_metric = (p, a) -> p != a, final = zeros(1001, 61))) for (name, p) in (("nominal", nominal), ("robust", robust)) println(name, ": collision ", round(collision(p, m); sigdigits = 3), " (complies), ", round(collision(p, worse); sigdigits = 3), " (80%), changes ", round(advisory_changes(p); digits = 3)) end @assert collision(robust, worse) < collision(nominal, worse) # Simple threshold policies: altitude thresholds 50, 100, 150, 200 m, time 30 s. pts = [[collision(ca_simple_policy(m; h_thresh = h), m), advisory_changes(ca_simple_policy(m; h_thresh = h))] for h in (50, 100, 150, 200)] println("on the Pareto front: ", pareto_front(permutedims(hcat(pts...)))) ``` ::: ### Adversarial analysis ::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"} ## Python ```python def adversary(model, policy, lam=None): """Solve the adversarial problem for a fixed policy (ADM §14.5). The adversary picks each transition's outcome (compliance and noise branch). Its step reward is our cost plus lam * log T(branch), and it also collects our collision cost at t_col = 0 (eq. 14.15). With lam=None it looks for the most likely failure instead (eq. 14.16): step reward log T(branch), 0 for ending in a collision, -inf for not. Returns (W, choice): W[a_prev, i_h, i_hdot] is the adversary's best total from each state at t_col = T_START, and choice[t] (same shape) is the index of its best branch at t_col = t, in the order of outcomes(). Deterministic search, so dynamic programming is exact. """ hit = collided(model) if lam is None: W = np.where(hit > 0, 0.0, -np.inf) W = np.repeat(W[None], 3, axis=0) else: W = np.repeat(model.collision_cost * hit[None], 3, axis=0) a_prev = np.arange(3)[:, None, None] i = np.arange(W.shape[1])[:, None] j = np.arange(W.shape[2])[None, :] choice = [None] for t in range(1, T_START + 1): # best[a, k]: value of branch k after advisory a, for every state. best = np.array([[(np.log(p) if lam is None else lam * np.log(p)) + W[a][ih, idd] for ih, idd, p in outcomes(model, a)] for a in range(3)]) a = policy[t] # (a_prev, n_h, n_hdot) per_branch = best[a, :, i, j] # (a_prev, n_h, n_hdot, k) choice.append(per_branch.argmax(axis=-1)) W = per_branch.max(axis=-1) if lam is not None: W = W + model.change_cost * (a != a_prev) return W, choice def replay(model, policy, choice, h, hdot): """Follow the adversary's choices from one start (h, hdot). Returns a list of (t_col, h, hdot, advisory, nu) per step, then the final (0, h, hdot, None, None).""" a_prev, steps = 0, [] for t in range(T_START, 0, -1): ih, idd = _index(model, h, hdot) a = int(policy[t][a_prev, ih, idd]) k = int(choice[t][a_prev, ih, idd]) # Recover the branch: compliance outer loop, noise inner loop. branches = [(c, nu) for c, pc in ((True, model.compliance), (False, 1 - model.compliance)) if pc > 0 for nu, _ in model.noise_outcomes()] comply, nu = branches[k] acc = int(accel(model, np.array(hdot), a)) if comply else 0 steps.append((t, h, hdot, a, nu)) h, hdot, a_prev = h + hdot, hdot + acc + nu, a steps.append((0, h, hdot, None, None)) return steps ``` ## Julia ```{.julia .snippet} using ADM m = CAModel() policy, _ = ca_optimal_policy(m) simple = ca_simple_policy(m) # W[a_prev, i, j]: best log-probability of a path that ends in a collision (eq. 14.16). # Each gust (probability ¼) is half as likely as calm air (½), so a path with k gusts # has log-probability 40 log ½ - k log 2. function gusts_needed(policy) W = ca_most_likely_failure(m, policy) Ws = W[1, (-200:200) .+ (m.h_max + 1), (-10:10) .+ (m.hdot_max + 1)] # starts; a_prev = none return round.(Int, (CA_T_START * log(0.5) .- Ws) ./ log(2)) end g_opt, g_simple = gusts_needed(policy), gusts_needed(simple) println("optimal policy: at least $(minimum(g_opt)) gusts from any start") println("simple policy: $(round(100 * sum(g_simple .== 0) / length(g_simple); digits = 1))% of starts fail in calm air") @assert minimum(g_opt) >= 3 && any(g_simple .== 0) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reading the Julia code (for Python programmers)"} - **`policy[t][a_prev, ca_index(m, h, ḣ)...]`**: `...` splats the tuple of two indices into the indexing call, like `policy[t][(a_prev,) + idx]` in Python. - **`risk[t]` is the risk at $t_{\text{col}} = t - 1$**: Julia arrays start at 1, so the list of values from $t_{\text{col}} = 0$ to 40 is indexed 1 to 41. - **Advisories are 1, 2, 3** (none, descend, climb) in Julia and 0, 1, 2 in Python. - **`first.(runs)`** applies `first` to each tuple, like `[r[0] for r in runs]`. - **`import Distributions`** with qualified names avoids clashes with other packages' exports (§6.1 of the site's conventions). ::: ### Run them ::: {#9df6a4bc .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} m = ca.Model() policy, cost = ca.optimal_policy(m) exact = ca.start_average(m, ca.evaluate(m, policy)) rng = np.random.default_rng(7) starts = ca.sample_starts(10_000, rng) h_end, _, _ = ca.simulate(m, policy, *starts, rng) direct = mc_estimate(np.abs(h_end) < ca.COLLISION_H) risk = ca.evaluate(ca.Model(noise=3), policy, history=True) # a rough model's risk-to-go h_end, _, log_w = ca.simulate(m, policy, *starts, rng, guide=risk) guided = importance_estimate(np.abs(h_end) < ca.COLLISION_H, log_w) ``` ::: ::: {#47f2d002 .cell execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` exact 6.416e-04; How many direct simulations are needed for a relative standard error of 20%? How many failures would you expect to see? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} The relative SE of a 0/1 estimate is $\sqrt{(1-p)/(np)}$. Setting it to 0.2 gives $n = (1-p)/(0.04\,p) \approx 2.5 \times 10^6$. That's about $np = 25$ failures. In general, relative error $\approx 1/\sqrt{\text{failures}}$: 25 failures for 20%, 100 for 10%, whatever $p$ is. Rarer events just take longer to produce those failures. ::: **Problem 2: an importance weight.** A proposal changes a coin with $P(\text{heads}) = 0.1$ into one with $P'(\text{heads}) = 0.5$. In 5 flips we see H, T, T, H, T. What is the importance weight of this sequence? If the event of interest is "at least 2 heads", what does this one sample contribute to the estimate? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} Heads contributes $0.1/0.5 = 0.2$ and tails $0.9/0.5 = 1.8$. The weight is $0.2^2 \times 1.8^3 = 0.04 \times 5.832 = 0.233$. The event occurred, so the sample contributes $1 \times 0.233 = 0.233$ to the average. For comparison, the true $P(\ge 2 \text{ heads}) = 1 - 0.9^5 - 5(0.1)(0.9^4) \approx 0.081$. Samples with more heads get smaller weights, and samples with fewer heads (which rarely satisfy the event) get larger ones, and on average they balance. ::: **Problem 3: the ideal proposal.** A fair six-sided die is rolled. You want $\mathbb{E}[f(X)]$ with $f(x) = x$ if $x \ge 5$ and 0 otherwise. What is the optimal proposal, and what does each of its samples contribute? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} By @eq-optimal-proposal, $P^*(x) \propto |f(x)|\,P(x)$: $P^*(5) \propto 5/6$ and $P^*(6) \propto 6/6$, so $P^*(5) = 5/11$ and $P^*(6) = 6/11$. A sample of 5 contributes $f(5)\,P(5)/P^*(5) = 5 \times (1/6)/(5/11) = 11/6$. A sample of 6 contributes $6 \times (1/6)/(6/11) = 11/6$. Every sample gives the exact answer $\mathbb{E}[f] = (5 + 6)/6 = 11/6$: zero variance. Building $P^*$ required knowing the answer, the normalizing sum 11/6, which is the catch. ::: **Problem 4: a robust choice.** In one state, action $x$ has expected costs 1.0 under model A and 3.0 under model B, and action $y$ has 1.8 under both. Which action does the nominal policy (model A only) choose, and which does robust dynamic programming choose? When is the robust choice a mistake? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} The nominal policy picks $x$ (1.0 < 1.8). Robust DP scores each action by its worst model: $x \to 3.0$, $y \to 1.8$, and picks $y$. If model A is almost always right, the robust choice pays 0.8 extra nearly every time to insure against a rare case. Robust DP ignores how likely each model is; if the models' probabilities are known, minimizing the expected cost over them (a belief over models, as in Part IV) can be the better choice. ::: **Problem 5: when does the adversary give up?** From some start, the most likely collision needs $k$ gusts, each half as likely as calm air, and our only cost is 1 for a collision. For which $\lambda$ does the adversary of @eq-adversarial choose the collision over the calm-air path? Check against the explorer's start (60, 0), whose most likely collision needs 7 gusts. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} The collision path's log-likelihood is $k \log 2$ below the calm path's. The adversary prefers the collision when $1 > \lambda k \log 2$, that is $\lambda < 1/(k \log 2)$. For $k = 7$: $\lambda < 1/(7 \times 0.693) \approx 0.21$. In the explorer, the start (60, 0) collides for $\lambda \le 0.1$ and stays safe at 0.3, as predicted. (Advisory changes add 0.01 each to the adversary's reward, which barely moves the threshold.) At very small $\lambda$ the adversary uses many more gusts than needed, because it also gains 0.01 for each advisory change it provokes. ::: ## Recap 1. **A performance metric is an expected trajectory score; additive scores are value functions (@eq-metric, @eq-additive).** *Why it matters:* any policy evaluation method from Chapters 7–9 doubles as a validation tool. Here exact evaluation gave the true collision probability, 6\.42e\-04, against which every estimate was checked. 2. **Every simulated estimate needs an error bar, and rare events need relative ones (@eq-standard-error).** *Why it matters:* relative error is about one over the square root of the number of failures observed. 10,000 encounters with 5 collisions gave a 45% relative error. 3. **Importance sampling makes rare events common, then reweights (@eq-importance, @eq-optimal-proposal).** *Why it matters:* a proposal guided by an approximate risk-to-go matched about 63 times as many direct samples. An over-aggressive proposal was worse than none. Chapter 3's likelihood weighting is the same idea. 4. **Policies are only as good as their models: stress-test them, and optimize against the worst case if needed (@eq-robust).** *Why it matters:* 80% pilot compliance made the optimal policy's collision risk 6 times higher. Uncertainty about the model itself is the theme of Part III. 5. **Trade analysis separates dominated designs from real choices (@eq-pareto).** *Why it matters:* the Pareto front shows what is achievable. Here every simple policy was beaten by an optimized one on both safety and alerts. 6. **Adversarial analysis turns validation into search for the most likely failure (@eq-adversarial).** *Why it matters:* it produces concrete, reviewable failure stories, like the late and too-weak climb above, and finds flaws, like the simple policy's calm-air collisions, that random testing may take a long time to hit. ## Cheat sheet & connections | Name | Formula | Ref | |---|---|---| | Performance metric | $f(\pi) = \mathbb{E}_\tau[f_{\text{traj}}(\tau)]$, $P(\tau) = b(s_1)\prod_t T(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, \pi(s_t))$ | @eq-metric | | Additive metric | $f(\pi) = \sum_s f_{\text{state}}(s)\, b(s)$ by policy evaluation | @eq-additive | | ★ Standard error | $\hat\sigma/\sqrt n$; relative: $\hat\sigma/(\hat\mu\sqrt n)$ | @eq-standard-error | | ★ Importance sampling | $\frac1n\sum_i f_{\text{traj}}(\tau^{(i)})\,P(\tau^{(i)})/P'(\tau^{(i)})$, $\tau^{(i)} \sim P'$ | @eq-importance | | Optimal proposal | $P^* \propto |f_{\text{traj}}|\,P$; per step $P'(\nu \mid s) \propto P(\nu)\,\hat U(s')$ | @eq-optimal-proposal | | Robust Bellman update | $\max_a \min_i (R_i + \gamma \sum_{s'} T_i U_k)$ | @eq-robust | | Pareto dominance | no worse on every metric, better on one | @eq-pareto | | Adversarial reward | $-R(s, \pi(s)) + \lambda \log T(s' \mid s, \pi(s))$ | @eq-adversarial | : Key equations from this page (★ = well-known by name). {#tbl-cheatsheet} **Common pitfalls** - **Reporting a rare-event estimate without its relative error.** Three failures in 10,000 trials is an estimate with an error bar about as wide as the estimate itself. - **A proposal that is too aggressive.** Weights that vary over orders of magnitude give estimates that are unbiased on average but wrong in almost every run. Watch the effective sample size. - **A proposal that misses part of the failure space.** If $P'$ can't produce some failures, the estimate is biased low, with no warning. Keep every outcome possible (the small constant in the guided proposal). - **Validating on the planning model only.** A policy exploits its model's assumptions, such as perfect compliance. Evaluate on models it wasn't optimized for. - **Treating the most likely failure as the only failure.** It is the single most probable failing path.
